legend: For an array of integers a%%ZSMJ0%%, a triplet of elements is defined by 3 distinct indices (ai,aj,ak)%%ZSMJ1%%, and their order does not matter.
Consider the triplets from a%%ZSMJ2%% that sum to zero.
For example, the array a=[1,1,1,2,−2,0]%%ZSMJ3%% has 4%%ZSMJ4%% triplets that sum to zero: (a1,a2,a5)%%ZSMJ5%%, (a1,a3,a5)%%ZSMJ6%%, (a2,a3,a5)%%ZSMJ7%%, and (a4,a5,a6)%%ZSMJ8%%.
Given an integer k%%ZSMJ9%%, construct an array of integers a%%ZSMJ10%% such that exactly k%%ZSMJ11%% triplets of elements from a%%ZSMJ12%% sum to zero.
Your array must have size at most 5000%%ZSMJ13%%.
input: The single line of the input contains an integer k%%ZSMJ14%% (0≤k≤109%%ZSMJ15%%) — the required number of triplets that sum to zero.
output: On the first line, output a single integer n%%ZSMJ16%% (0≤n≤5000%%ZSMJ17%%) — the size of a%%ZSMJ18%%.
On the second line, output n%%ZSMJ19%% space-separated integers a1,…,an%%ZSMJ20%% (−109≤ai≤109%%ZSMJ21%%).
If there are multiple arrays satisfying these conditions, output any of them.
It can be shown that a valid answer always exists.
note: In sample 1, no triples in the array a%%ZSMJ22%% sum to zero.
In sample 2, the only triple that sums to zero is (a2,a4,a5)%%ZSMJ23%%.
